questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: state the ordering precondition of a halving search
questions.stem: A parts catalog is searched with a helper that halves its index range at every step. Which precondition must hold for that helper to report correct results?

options.text: The catalog codes are in ascending order by code
The catalog codes were added in the order they arrived
options.misconception: arrival order steers the halving

options.text: The catalog codes contain no repeated values
options.misconception: duplicates make halving illegal

options.text: The catalog codes were stored in a two-column layout
options.misconception: a two-column layout is required

questions.explanation: Halving discards half the window, and that is sound only if the discarded half is provably on one side of the target, which is a property of sorted storage. The tempting answer is the no-duplicates rule because duplicates feel like an edge case, but repeats do not break the logic and arrival order stops mattering the moment the array is sorted.
questions.hint: Ask what lets the helper throw away a whole half.

questions.learningObjective: select the search that needs no ordering precondition
questions.stem: A volunteer needs a routine that finds a locker number no matter what order the numbers happen to be stored in. Which search fits without any ordering precondition?

options.text: A linear scan that tests each slot from the first to the last
A halving search that narrows the window down to one half
options.misconception: halving works on unsorted data too

options.text: A midpoint search that compares against the middle element
options.misconception: comparing the middle finds any layout

options.text: A merge of two sorted halves into a single sorted array
options.misconception: merging repairs disorder by itself

questions.explanation: A linear scan makes no claim about the values surrounding the slot it inspects, so it is correct on any arrangement and simply pays a full pass in the worst case. The tempting answer is the halving search because it looks more sophisticated, but each of its decisions assumes the discarded half cannot hold the target, and on unsorted data that assumption produces confidently wrong answers.
questions.hint: Ask which search never reasons about a neighbouring slot.

questions.learningObjective: count the outer passes of an insertion sort
questions.stem: An insertion sort holds one value in a key variable and slides larger entries one slot to the right. For an array of n values, how many times does the outer loop body run?

options.text: exactly n - 1 times, once per value after the first
exactly n times, once for every value in the array
options.misconception: the first value also needs a pass

options.text: exactly 1 time, because one pass sorts the whole array
options.misconception: insertion sort needs no repeated passes

options.text: exactly n divided by 2 times, one pass per pair
options.misconception: each pass handles a pair of values

questions.explanation: After the first iteration the slot holding the key is already correctly placed relative to everything before it, so iteration i only has to insert the value at index i into the sorted prefix and the loop stops at n - 1. options.misconception: indexOf is restricted to strings

questions.learningObjective: judge when a zero seed is safe for a maximum scan
questions.stem: A routine finds the largest of several values by starting a variable at 0 and replacing it whenever a larger value appears. When is that seed safe?

options.text: only when no value in the list is greater than zero
always, because zero is the neutral starting value
options.misconception: zero is the identity for a maximum scan

options.text: only when the list is sorted in ascending order
options.misconception: sorted order rescues a zero seed

options.text: only when the list holds at least two values
options.misconception: the seed needs a minimum list size

questions.explanation: A maximum scan keeps the largest value seen so far, so the seed is trustworthy only if nothing in the data sits above it; the moment a positive value appears the seed must be below every candidate, and with all-negative data 0 survives and the reported maximum is wrong. questions.stem: Trace this halving search over data that was never sorted: int[] data = {5, 9, 1, 7, 3}; int lo = 0; int hi = data.length - 1; int found = -1; while (lo <= hi) { int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (data[mid] == 5) { found = mid; break; } if (data[mid] > 5) { hi = mid - 1; } else { lo = mid + 1; } } System.out.print(found); What prints?

the middle slot is checked on the first step
the window lands on the target after one narrowing

questions.learningObjective: compute the number of outer passes for a given length
questions.stem: A sorting routine increments a counter once per outer loop body: int[] data = {9, 4, 7, 1}; int passes = 0; for (int i = 1; i < data.length; i++) { int key = data[i]; int j = i - 1; while (j >= 0 && data[j] > key) { data[j + 1] = data[j]; j--; } data[j + 1] = key; passes++; } System.out.print(passes); What value is printed?
questions.explanation: The loop starts at i = 1 and runs while i is below the length of 4, so the body executes for i = 1, 2 and 3 and the counter ends at 3. The tempting value is 4 because the array holds four values, but the first slot is already in place with nothing to its left, so it never needs a pass of its own and the counter measures insertions rather than elements.

questions.stem: Trace this shift count: int[] data = {5, 2, 4}; int shifts = 0; for (int i = 1; i < data.length; i++) { int key = data[i]; int j = i - 1; while (j >= 0 && data[j] > key) { data[j + 1] = data[j]; j--; shifts++; } data[j + 1] = key; } System.out.print(shifts); What prints?

options.misconception: each outer pass counts as one shift
only the first pass moves a value right
the array holds three slots so five moves fit

questions.explanation: Inserting 2 slides 5 one slot right, and inserting 4 slides 5 one slot right as well, while 2 already sits left of 4 and does not move, so the counter reaches 2. a repeated letter still appends a new entry

it prints copied, because the last read is harmless
options.misconception: a trailing iteration is always valid

options.text: it prints copied, because reads past the end are zero
options.misconception: out-of-range reads return a default

options.text: An out-of-bounds error, because the array has three slots
options.misconception: the length of an int array is three

questions.stem: This counter totals every shift made while sorting: int[] data = {4, 3, 2, 1}; int shifts = 0; for (int i = 1; i < data.length; i++) { int key = data[i]; int j = i - 1; while (j >= 0 && data[j] > key) { data[j + 1] = data[j]; j--; shifts++; } data[j + 1] = key; } System.out.print(shifts); What value is printed?
questions.explanation: Each pass slides every value larger than the key, so the counts are 1, 2 and 3 for i = 1, 2 and 3 and the total is 6. The tempting value is 3, one per pass, but a pass can move many values when the input arrives in reverse order, and the very same code records no shifts at all on data that is already sorted, so the work tracks disorder rather than length alone.
questions.hint: Add the number of values each pass actually moves.

questions.learningObjective: seed a range minimum from inside the range

options.text: data[lo]
data[0]
options.misconception: index zero starts every scan

options.text: data[hi]
options.misconception: the upper bound is the right seed

options.text: data.length
options.misconception: the length seeds the comparison

questions.explanation: The seed has to be a value the loop actually tests, and data[lo] is the first slot the loop visits, so every later value is compared against a candidate drawn from the range itself. The tempting answer is data[0] out of habit from a whole-array scan, but that slot lies outside the requested range and can be smaller than everything in it, in which case the true minimum is never reported at all.
questions.hint: Ask which slot the loop visits first.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: select the single repair that makes a halving search sound
questions.stem: A search reports false negatives on data loaded in file order. int[] data = {9, 4, 7, 1, 6}; int target = 6; int lo = 0; int hi = data.length - 1; int found = -1; while (lo <= hi) { int mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if (data[mid] == target) { found = mid; break; } if (data[mid] > target) { hi = mid - 1; } else { lo = mid + 1; } } Which single change makes this input trustworthy?

options.text: Sort the array once, before the halving loop begins
Start lo at 1 so the first slot is never discarded
options.misconception: the first slot is the one lost here

options.text: Replace the halving loop with a scan over every slot
options.misconception: halving can never be repaired

options.text: Search for target plus one to land on the right value
options.misconception: the target needs shifting by one

questions.explanation: Every halving decision rests on sorted order, and once the data is sorted this same code reports index 2 for 6 in the repaired array, so sorting is the only change that makes the existing logic sound. The tempting answers each alter the search rather than the data, and a full scan does return the right index but abandons the halving efficiency entirely, while shifting the target corrupts the value being sought.
questions.hint: Ask whether the comparison holds for the data in this order.

questions.learningObjective: choose the loop bound that includes the upper limit

options.misconception: an exclusive bound is the natural reading
the index should run above the bound
any inequality reaches the bound

questions.explanation: The bounds are inclusive positions, so the loop must keep going while the index is at or below the upper limit; with the strict form the slot holding the final letter is never tested and the count for "abra" comes out as one instead of two. The tempting strict form reads more naturally as a half-open range, but here the named bound is the last index to visit, not one past it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the slot at the upper bound should be counted.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.learningObjective: judge which stated conditions are genuine routine preconditions
questions.stem: Four claims about routine preconditions sit on a review sheet. Which of them describe a real condition that the caller must satisfy? Select all that apply.

options.text: A halving search requires the data to be in ascending order
A maximum scan seeded at 0 requires non-positive data
A copy loop over src.length needs src to be sorted
options.misconception: copying depends on the order of elements

options.text: A frequency map built with indexOf needs distinct letters
options.misconception: counting only works on unique keys

questions.explanation: A precondition is a condition on the input that the routine cannot establish for itself, and both sorted order and a seed that bounds the data are exactly that, since violating either makes the routine answer confidently and wrongly. The tempting answers name conditions that are irrelevant, because transferring elements and counting repeated letters both work in any order and over any set of values, duplicates included.
questions.hint: Ask which conditions the routine's own logic relies on.
